## Overview

The weak and strong **laws of large numbers** are fundamental results in
probability theory. Writing $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$, they describe the long-run
behaviour of the **sample mean**
$$
\bar{X}_n=\frac{S_{n}}{n}=\frac{{X_{1}+\dots+X_{n}}}{n}.
$$
The **weak law (WLLN)** states that $\bar{X}_n$ converges
[[convergence-in-probability|in probability]] to the expected value, and the
**strong law (SLLN)** that it converges
[[convergence-almost-surely|almost surely]]. The weak laws are proved with the
[[chebyshev-inequality]] and the strong law additionally uses the
[[borel-cantelli-lemma]]. There are many versions with different strength of
assumptions.

## Weak Laws

The simplest result is for i.i.d. random variables with finite variance.

:::{.theorem data-title="Weak Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $X_{1}, \dots, X_{n}$ be i.i.d. with finite mean $\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mu$ and
finite variance $\operatorname{Var}(X_{i})=\sigma^2<\infty$. Then the sample
mean converges in probability and in $L_2$ to $\mu$,
$$
\frac{S_{n}}{n} \stackrel{L_{2}~\&~\mathbb{P}}{\to}\mu\quad (n\to \infty),
$$
that is, for every $\epsilon>0$,
$\lim_{ n \to \infty }\mathbb{P}(|\bar{X}_{n}-\mu|<\epsilon)=1$.

:::

:::{.proof}

First, $\mathbb{E}\left[ S_{n}/n \right]= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mu=\mu$ and
$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(  \frac{S_{n}}{n} \right)= \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_{i})= \frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$
Fixing $\epsilon>0$, the [[chebyshev-inequality]] gives
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(  \left| \frac{S_{n}}{n} -\mu\right| \geq \epsilon \right)\leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon ^2}\to 0\quad(n\to\infty).
$$
Since $\mathbb{E}|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n\to0$ we also have $L_2$ convergence.

:::

The assumptions can be weakened to uncorrelated random variables with bounded
variance.

:::{.theorem data-title="$L_2$ Weak Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \dots$ be uncorrelated random variables with
$\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_{i})\leq C<\infty$. Then
$$
\frac{S_{n}}{n} \stackrel{L_{2}~\&~\mathbb{P}}{\to}\mu\quad (n\to \infty).
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

By uncorrelatedness the variances add, so
$$
\mathbb{E}\left\lvert   \frac{S_{n}}{n}-\mu  \right\rvert ^2=\operatorname{Var}\left(  \frac{S_{n}}{n} \right)=n^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(X_{i})\leq  n^{-2}\cdot n\cdot C \to 0.
$$
Convergence in probability follows from the [[chebyshev-inequality]] (or from
the fact that $L^2$ convergence implies convergence in probability, see
[[convergence-in-lp-norm]]).

:::

The most general version gives conditions under which the sample mean,
centred by a suitable truncated mean, converges in probability.

:::{.theorem data-title="General Weak Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $\{  X_{n} \}$ be independent random variables such that

1. $\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{P}(\lvert  X_{j} \rvert>n)\to 0$ as $n \to \infty$;
   and
2. $\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbb{E}[X_{j}^2 \mathbb{1}_{\lvert X_{j} \rvert \leq n}]\to 0$
   as $n \to \infty$.

Define $a_{n}:=\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_{j}\mathbb{1}_{\lvert X_{j} \rvert\leq n}]$.
Then $\frac{{S_n-a_n}}{n}\stackrel{\mathbb{P}}{\to}0$ as $n \to \infty$.

:::

:::{.proof}

Truncate: let $T_n=\sum_{j=1}^nX_j\mathbb{1}_{\lvert X_{j} \rvert\leq n}$, so
$\mathbb{E}T_n=a_n$. Then
$\mathbb{P}(S_n\neq T_n)\leq\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbb{P}(\lvert X_j\rvert>n)\to0$ by
condition 1. By independence and condition 2,
$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{T_n}{n}\right)\leq\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbb{E}[X_{j}^2 \mathbb{1}_{\lvert X_{j} \rvert \leq n}]\to0,
$$
so the [[chebyshev-inequality]] gives $\mathbb{P}(|T_n-a_n|>\epsilon n)\to0$ for
all $\epsilon>0$. Finally
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{|S_n-a_n|}{n}>\epsilon\right)\leq\mathbb{P}(S_n\neq T_n)+\mathbb{P}(|T_n-a_n|>\epsilon n)\to0.
$$

:::

Two classical versions follow from the general law. **Feller's WLLN** drops
the often restrictive first moment assumption.

:::{.theorem data-title="Feller's Weak Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $\{  X_{n} \}$ be i.i.d. with $\lim_{x \to \infty}x\mathbb{P}(\lvert  X_{1} \rvert>x)=0$.
Then
$$
\frac{S_{n}}{n}-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}\mathbb{1}_{\lvert X_{1} \rvert \leq  n}]\stackrel{\mathbb{P}}{\to}0\quad \text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

Condition 1 of the general law reads $n\mathbb{P}(|X_1|>n)\to0$, which is the
assumption. For condition 2 we need $\frac1n\mathbb{E}[X_1^2\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|\leq n}]\to0$. Writing
$\mathbb{E}[X_1^2\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|\leq n}]\leq\int_0^n2x\,\mathbb{P}(|X_1|>x)\,dx$
and using that $2x\mathbb{P}(|X_1|>x)\to0$, the Cesàro average
$\frac1n\int_0^n2x\,\mathbb{P}(|X_1|>x)\,dx\to0$. Finally
$a_n/n=\mathbb{E}[X_1\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|\leq n}]$.

:::

**Khinchine's WLLN** is the version for i.i.d. sequences with a finite first
moment.

:::{.theorem data-title="Khinchine's Weak Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $\{  X_{n} \}$ be i.i.d. with $\mathbb{E}[\lvert X_{1} \rvert]< \infty$ and
$\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]=\mu$. Then
$$
\frac{S_{n}}{n}\stackrel{\mathbb{P}}{\to}\mu\quad\text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

We check the conditions of the general law. Condition 1 holds since
$n\mathbb{P}(|X_1|>n)\leq\mathbb{E}[|X_1|\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|>n}]\to0$. For
condition 2 and any $\epsilon>0$,
$$
\frac1n\mathbb{E}[X_1^2\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|\leq n}]\leq\epsilon\,\mathbb{E}|X_1|+\mathbb{E}[|X_1|\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|>\epsilon n}]\to\epsilon\,\mathbb{E}|X_1|,
$$
and $\epsilon$ is arbitrary. Finally
$a_n/n=\mathbb{E}[X_1\mathbb{1}_{|X_1|\leq n}]\to\mu$ by the
[[dominated-convergence-theorem]].

:::

## Strong Laws

The **Strong Law of Large Numbers (SLLN)** is deeper than the weak law: the
sample average **converges almost surely** (with probability 1) to the expected
value. We start with the version requiring **finite second moments**.

:::{.theorem data-title="Strong Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $X_{1}, X_{2},\dots$ be i.i.d. with $\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mu$ and
$\mathbb{E}[X_{i}^2]<\infty$. Then
$$
\bar{X}_{n}\stackrel{a.s.}{\to}\mu\quad (n \to \infty),
$$
that is, $\mathbb{P}(\lim_{ n \to \infty }\bar{X}_{n}=\mu)=1$.

:::

:::{.proof}

Replacing $X_i$ by $X_i-\mu$ we may assume $\mu=0$; let
$\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$.

*Step 1: squares.* By the [[chebyshev-inequality]],
$\mathbb{P}(|S_{n^2}|>\epsilon n^2)\leq\sigma^2/(\epsilon^2n^2)$, which is
summable in $n$. By the [[borel-cantelli-lemma]], $S_{n^2}/n^2\to0$ a.s.

*Step 2: in between.* Let
$D_n=\max_{n^2\leq k<(n+1)^2}|S_k-S_{n^2}|$. Bounding the maximum by a sum over
the $2n+1$ indices, each term having second moment at most $2n\sigma^2$,
$\mathbb{E}D_n^2\leq(2n+1)2n\sigma^2\leq 6n^2\sigma^2$. Hence
$\mathbb{P}(D_n>\epsilon n^2)\leq6\sigma^2/(\epsilon^2n^2)$ is summable and
$D_n/n^2\to0$ a.s. by Borel-Cantelli.

For $n^2\leq k<(n+1)^2$ we then have
$|S_k|/k\leq(|S_{n^2}|+D_n)/n^2\to0$ a.s.

:::

Finally, the general version only needs pairwise independence and a finite
first moment.

:::{.theorem data-title="General Strong Law of Large Numbers (Etemadi)"}

Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \dots$ be pairwise independent identically distributed
random variables with $\mathbb{E}\lvert X_{1} \rvert<\infty$ and
$\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]=\mu$. Then
$$
\frac{S_{n}}{n}= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^nX_{i}}{n} \stackrel{a.s.}{\to}\mu\quad \text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
$$

:::

The proof combines truncation, the subsequence argument above with
geometrically growing indices, and the Borel-Cantelli lemma; see Etemadi
(1981) or Durrett.

## References

- R. Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*, Cambridge University Press.
- N. Etemadi, "An elementary proof of the strong law of large numbers", *Z.
  Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete* 55 (1981), 119-122.
